explanations.answer: Moth and rust destroy it and thieves steal it
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what Jesus says. Treasure on earth is where "moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal." Think of a cookie jar on an open counter. Something will get into it, and it won't be the moths.

explanations.answer: Tax collectors come and take half of it
explanations.explanation: I get why that one sounds believable, friend. Everybody has felt a bill take a bite out of what they earned. But Jesus never mentions tax collectors here. He names moth and rust, which destroy, and thieves, who break in and steal. Nobody in this verse sends a bill.

explanations.answer: Kings seize it to pay their armies
explanations.explanation: That would be a rough day, but it isn't what Jesus says. He never brings up kings or armies in this verse. He says earthly treasure is where "moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal." The trouble is small stuff chewing and rusting it, plus thieves.

True. Jesus says, "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." So your heart follows your treasure. I'd say that's worth checking, because I once watched a baker's eyes follow a fresh tray across a whole room.
It's actually true. Jesus says, "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." The heart goes where the treasure is. So whatever you're storing up, your heart is headed that way too.

Not quite, friend. Jesus doesn't say part of the body. He says, "if your eyes are bad, your whole body will be full of darkness." The darkness isn't a little corner. It fills the whole body, just like good eyes fill it with light.

False is right. Jesus says, "But if your eyes are bad, your whole body will be full of darkness." Not a patch of it. The whole body. It's the same "whole body" He used for the light in the verse before.

explanations.answer: He'll love one and hate the other
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says. "Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other." You can't split down the middle. One master ends up with your heart.

explanations.answer: He'll get worn out by both of them
explanations.explanation: Anyone who's juggled two bosses knows that feeling, friend. But Jesus doesn't say tired. He says the person will "hate the one and love the other," or be "devoted to the one and despise the other." He's talking about where the loyalty lands.

explanations.answer: He'll end up working for neither
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but that isn't in the verse. Jesus says the one who tries will "hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other." He still ends up serving one of them. His heart picks a side.
Money it is. Jesus says, "You cannot serve both God and money." He's been talking about treasure, and now He names the rival master. Notice He says both, and you can't have it that way.
Fame is a fair guess, since it's another thing people chase. But Jesus doesn't use that word here. He says, "You cannot serve both God and money." It lands right after all that talk about treasure.

Comfort feels close, friend, and I love a warm kitchen as much as anybody. But that's not the word Jesus picks. He says, "You cannot serve both God and money." After talking about treasure, money is the master He names.

explanations.answer: Life and body are worth more than food and clothes
explanations.explanation: That's His point. Jesus asks, "Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes?" He's saying you matter more than the things you're worrying over.

explanations.answer: Food and clothes are a waste of money
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says that, friend. He isn't calling food and clothes a waste. He asks, "Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes?" The point is that life and body are worth more than the worry.

explanations.answer: Fasting matters more than eating ever will
explanations.explanation: Fasting was in the part of the sermon just before this, but that's not what He's doing here. Jesus asks, "Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes?" He's not ranking fasting over eating. He's saying life and body are more than what you worry about.
Right. Jesus says the birds "do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them." The birds aren't doing the farm work. Their Father is the one feeding them.

explanations.answer: They take from the farmers' barns
explanations.explanation: Ha, I've known a few cookie thieves, but Jesus doesn't say birds raid barns. He says they don't gather into barns at all, and "yet your heavenly Father feeds them." The feeding comes from Him.

explanations.answer: They fly to wherever fields are full
explanations.explanation: That sounds sensible, friend, but it isn't in the verse. Jesus says the birds don't sow, reap or gather into barns, "and yet your heavenly Father feeds them." He gives the credit to the Father, not to the birds' travel plans.
It's the other way around. Jesus asks, "Are you not much more valuable than they?" So the birds are not worth more than you. You are worth much more than they are.

False is right. Jesus asks, "Are you not much more valuable than they?" He's saying the opposite of the claim. If the Father feeds the birds, you can count on Him for what you need, because you're worth much more.
Not this time, friend. Jesus says, "not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these." Solomon, the king with all that wealth, lost to a flower. Imagine the royal tailors hearing that.
Yes, false. Jesus says, "not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these." Solomon had more riches than any king on earth (1 Kings 10:23), and a lily still beat his wardrobe.

explanations.answer: He will much more clothe you
explanations.explanation: That's the answer. Jesus says, "If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, will He not much more clothe you…" If He dresses grass, He'll dress you.

explanations.answer: He wants you to dress plainly
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say anything about plain clothes, friend. His point is about how God treats grass: He clothes it, and it's gone tomorrow. So "will He not much more clothe you…" The point is that God will provide.

explanations.answer: He expects you to make your own
explanations.explanation: I'd be in trouble if that were the lesson, since I stamp cookies and don't sew. But Jesus never says that. He says God clothes the grass, and then asks, "will He not much more clothe you…" The clothing comes from God.

Need is right. Jesus says the Gentiles strive after these things, "and your heavenly Father knows that you need them." He isn't brushing off food, drink and clothes. He says your Father knows you need them.
Close in sound, friend, but not what He says. Jesus says, "your heavenly Father knows that you need them." It isn't about what you've earned. It's about what the Father knows you need.
Not quite. Jesus doesn't say you waste these things. He says, "your heavenly Father knows that you need them." Food, drink and clothes are things your Father knows you need.

explanations.answer: The kingdom of God and His righteousness
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, "But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness…" After telling them what not to chase, He gives them something to chase. Put that first.

explanations.answer: The treasures of earth and their glory
explanations.explanation: That's the very thing He's been steering them away from, friend. Back in verse 19 He said not to store up treasures on earth. What He tells them to seek first is "the kingdom of God and His righteousness."

explanations.answer: The favor of men and their praise
explanations.explanation: People's approval is a tempting thing to chase, I'll give you that. But that's not on Jesus' list here. He says, "But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness…" That comes first.

True. Jesus says, "But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you." The "things" are the food, drink and clothes He's been talking about. He puts the kingdom first and the rest follows.

It's actually true, friend. Jesus says, "But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you." The "things" are the same ones He named when He told them not to worry.
Trouble is right. Jesus says, "Today has enough trouble of its own." Each day brings its own load. You don't have to carry tomorrow's too.
I wish it read that way, friend. But Jesus says, "Today has enough trouble of its own." He's telling them not to pile tomorrow's worry on top of today's.
Time makes sense, since we never have enough. But Jesus uses a different word. He says, "Today has enough trouble of its own." That's why He says not to worry about tomorrow.
